rules.statement: Do not add a separate boolean or flag to control a capability that a supported-values list (such as `response_types_supported`) already governs; discovery, registration and request validation must all read that one list.
rules.why: A second switch can disagree with the list, so a flow ends up advertised and registrable but refused at every request, which breaks the rule that advertisement and enforcement share one source.
rules.check: Look for new settings, options or checks that allow or block a protocol capability that a supported-values list also covers, or for code paths where discovery, registration and enforcement read different settings for the same capability.

rules.statement: When the authorization endpoint refuses a response type, return `unsupported_response_type` if the server or tenant list forbids it, and `unauthorized_client` only if just the client's list forbids it.
rules.why: RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1 calls for `unsupported_response_type` when the server side does not support the response type, and the error code should show which scope imposed the restriction.
rules.check: Look for authorization-request validation that returns `unauthorized_client` for every response-type refusal, or that does not tell a tenant/server-level refusal apart from a client-level one.

rules.statement: Keep the secure-by-default supported response types at `code` only, so that by default the authorization endpoint returns no access token in the authorization response.
rules.why: RFC 9700 §2.1.2 says clients SHOULD NOT use response types that issue access tokens in the authorization response.
rules.check: Look for default or baseline `response_types_supported` values that include any response type containing `token`.

rules.statement: When you retire a persisted setting, add a one-time data migration that rewrites each stored document into an equivalent expression of what the setting meant; do not just delete the setting, and do not translate it at read time.
rules.why: Dropping a restrictive value would silently loosen what the document allowed. A one-time rewrite also keeps the retired name out of the runtime entirely.
rules.check: Look for a removed setting descriptor or key that has no matching migration, for a migration that deletes the setting without carrying its restrictive values into the remaining settings, or for read-time compatibility code that keeps interpreting the retired name.

rules.statement: A migration that retires a setting must leave documents with invalid values for that setting unchanged, so they keep failing when read; it must not guess what the operator meant.
rules.why: Guessing what the operator intended could change behavior silently. Leaving the document failing makes an operator correct it.
rules.check: Look for migration code that coerces, defaults or drops values that were already invalid under the old model instead of skipping those documents.

rules.statement: Any migration that rewrites stored settings documents must give each rewritten document a new concurrency token, the same as any other settings write.
rules.why: A rewritten document is a settings write, and keeping the old token would defeat optimistic concurrency checks.
rules.check: Look for data migrations that update settings documents without regenerating their concurrency token.

rules.statement: If configuration names a retired or unknown setting, stop the host at startup with an error that names the configuration path; do not ignore the setting.
rules.why: Setting names are a closed vocabulary. Silently ignoring a retired setting could loosen restrictions the operator expects to be in force.
rules.check: Look for setting-binding code that skips unknown or retired setting names, or that fails without naming the configuration path.
